text:
The presented methods cover the main aspects of problem solving in propositional and first-order logic. Mastering these methods, combined with a good knowledge of fundamental logical laws, allows addressing a wide variety of problems in software modeling and verification.
Key points:

Always start by understanding the logical structure of the problem
Choose the method adapted to the problem type (validation, modeling, satisfaction)
Systematically apply logical laws in transformations
Verify the consistency of found solutions
Clearly document each step of the reasoning

title: Series 3
text:
Method 1: WP for Assignment
For an assignment x := e, substitute variable x with expression e in postcondition \(\psi\):
\[ \mathrm{WP}(x := e, \psi) = \psi[x \leftarrow e] \]
Method 2: WP for Conditional
For an instruction if B then c_1 else c_2, combine the WP of both branches, conditioned by B and ¬B:
\[ \mathrm{WP}(\text{if } B \text{ then } c_1 \text{ else } c_2, \psi) = (B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_1, \psi)) \land (\neg B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_2, \psi)) \]
Method 3: Consideration of Safety Conditions
When the program contains a partial operation (e.g., division), safety conditions (e.g., denominator non-zero) must be explicitly added to the WP.





Method 4: Validity via Logical Implication
A triple \(\{P\}\ c\ \{Q\}\) is valid if and only if the precondition \(P\) implies the WP of program \(c\) for postcondition \(Q\):
\[ \{P\}\ c\ \{Q\} \text{ is valid } \quad \text{iff} \quad P \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c, Q) \ \text{is true}. \]
All safety conditions (e.g., non-division by zero) must also be verified.
Method 5: Refinement with Additional Precondition
If the computed WP is not automatically verified, we can propose a stronger precondition \(P\) that makes the implication valid.





Method 6: Structural Induction on Programs
To prove a property about \(\mathrm{WP}\) for all programs, proceed by induction on the program structure:

Base case: elementary instructions (assignment).

Induction steps: sequential composition, conditional, loop.






Method 7: Common Logical Transformations

Implication elimination: \(A \Rightarrow B \equiv \neg A \lor B\)

De Morgan’s laws: \(\neg (A \land B) \equiv \neg A \lor \neg B\), \(\neg (A \lor B) \equiv \neg A \land \neg B\)

Distributivity: \(A \land (B \lor C) \equiv (A \land B) \lor (A \land C)\)








WP Rules

\(\mathrm{WP}(x := e, \psi) = \psi[x \leftarrow e]\)

\(\mathrm{WP}(\text{if } B \text{ then } c_1 \text{ else } c_2, \psi) = (B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_1, \psi)) \land (\neg B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_2, \psi))\)

Hoare Triple Validity
\[ \{P\}\ c\ \{Q\} \text{ valid } \iff P \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c, Q) \]
Safety Conditions
For any division a/b, add the condition \(b \neq 0\) to the WP.
Useful Logic Laws

Implication: \(A \Rightarrow B \equiv \neg A \lor B\)

Distributivity of \(\land\) over \(\lor\) and vice versa

Equivalence: \((A \Rightarrow (B \land C)) \equiv (A \Rightarrow B) \land (A \Rightarrow C)\)

Structural Induction

Base: verify the property for simple instructions.

Induction: assume the property for subprograms, prove it for compositions.








Context: Compute \(\mathrm{WP}(f, \psi_1)\) for the program
\[ f(a,b) = \text{if } (a > 2) \text{ then } res := a \text{ else } res := b \text{ endif} \]
with \(\psi_1 : res \geq 0\).
Application:

Apply the conditional rule:
\[ \mathrm{WP}(f, \psi_1) = (a > 2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(res := a, \psi_1)) \land (\neg (a > 2) \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(res := b, \psi_1)) \]

Compute the WP of assignments (Method 1):

\(\mathrm{WP}(res := a, \psi_1) = \psi_1[res \leftarrow a] = a \geq 0\)

\(\mathrm{WP}(res := b, \psi_1) = \psi_1[res \leftarrow b] = b \geq 0\)


Combine:
\[ \mathrm{WP}(f, \psi_1) = (a > 2 \Rightarrow a \geq 0) \land (\neg (a > 2) \Rightarrow b \geq 0) \]
i.e., \[ (a > 2 \Rightarrow a \geq 0) \land (a \leq 2 \Rightarrow b \geq 0). \]





Context: Verify if \(\{P_2\}\ f\ \{\psi_2\}\) is valid, with \(P_2 := \mathbf{T}\) (true) and \(\psi_2 : res \geq 42\).
Application:

We already computed:
\[ \mathrm{WP}(f, \psi_2) = (a > 2 \Rightarrow a \geq 42) \land (\neg (a > 2) \Rightarrow b \geq 42) \]

For validity, we need \(P_2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(f, \psi_2)\), i.e., \(\mathrm{WP}(f, \psi_2)\) must be true for all \(a,b\).

However, if \(a=3\) (so \(a>2\) true), we must have \(a \geq 42\), which is false. Therefore the implication is not true for all values.

Conclusion: The triple is not valid. However, it is satisfiable (e.g., with \(a=42, b=42\)).





Context: Compute \(\mathrm{WP}(g, \psi_3)\) for
\[ g(a,b) = \text{if } (a \geq b) \text{ then } res := a/b \text{ else } res := b/a \text{ endif} \]
with \(\psi_3 : res \geq 1\).
Application:

Apply the conditional rule:
\[ \mathrm{WP}(g, \psi_3) = (a \geq b \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(res := a/b, \psi_3)) \land (a < b \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(res := b/a, \psi_3)) \]

For each assignment with division, add the non-zero denominator condition (Method 3):

\(\mathrm{WP}(res := a/b, \psi_3) = (a/b \geq 1) \land (b \neq 0)\)

\(\mathrm{WP}(res := b/a, \psi_3) = (b/a \geq 1) \land (a \neq 0)\)


Therefore:
\[ \mathrm{WP}(g, \psi_3) = (a \geq b \Rightarrow (a/b \geq 1 \land b \neq 0)) \land (a < b \Rightarrow (b/a \geq 1 \land a \neq 0)) \]
i.e., separating the division conditions:
\[ (a \geq b \Rightarrow a/b \geq 1) \land (a < b \Rightarrow b/a \geq 1) \land (a \geq b \Rightarrow b \neq 0) \land (a < b \Rightarrow a \neq 0). \]





Context: Prove that for any program \(c\) and formulas \(P\), \(Q\),
\[ \mathrm{WP}(c, P \land Q) = \mathrm{WP}(c, P) \land \mathrm{WP}(c, Q). \]
Application (sketch of proof by structural induction):

Base case: \(c\) is an assignment \(x := e\).

\(\mathrm{WP}(x:=e, P \land Q) = (P \land Q)[x \leftarrow e] = P[x \leftarrow e] \land Q[x \leftarrow e]\)

\(\mathrm{WP}(x:=e, P) \land \mathrm{WP}(x:=e, Q) = P[x \leftarrow e] \land Q[x \leftarrow e]\)
→ Equality verified.

Conditional case: \(c = \text{if } B \text{ then } c_1 \text{ else } c_2\).

By induction hypothesis, \(\mathrm{WP}(c_1, P \land Q) = \mathrm{WP}(c_1, P) \land \mathrm{WP}(c_1, Q)\) (same for \(c_2\)).

Then:
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{WP}(c, P \land Q) &= (B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_1, P \land Q)) \land (\neg B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_2, P \land Q)) \\ &= (B \Rightarrow (\mathrm{WP}(c_1, P) \land \mathrm{WP}(c_1, Q))) \land (\neg B \Rightarrow (\mathrm{WP}(c_2, P) \land \mathrm{WP}(c_2, Q))) \\ &= (B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_1, P)) \land (B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_1, Q)) \land (\neg B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_2, P)) \land (\neg B \Rightarrow \mathrm{WP}(c_2, Q)) \\ &= \mathrm{WP}(c, P) \land \mathrm{WP}(c, Q) \end{aligned} \]
→ The property is preserved.

Other cases (sequence, loop) are treated similarly.

These methods are the basis of formal verification tools like Why3, where WPs are generated and verified automatically.

title: Series 5: Program Verification with Why3
text:
Description: In program verification, expected behavior is specified using logical assertions.

Precondition: Formula that must be true before program execution (assumptions about inputs).
Postcondition: Formula that must be true after execution (guarantees about outputs). These conditions are expressed in first-order logic, often with quantifiers over array indices and values.




Description: A loop invariant is a logical formula that remains true before and after each iteration of a loop. It allows reasoning about partial correctness and termination. For a while loop, the invariant must be:

true before the first iteration,
preserved by the loop body (if the invariant is true before the iteration and the guard condition is true, then it remains true after the iteration),
strong enough to imply the postcondition when the loop condition becomes false.




Description: To simplify specifications, predicates (boolean functions) are defined to encapsulate reusable properties (e.g., permutation, sorted). These predicates can be defined in Why3 and used in invariants, preconditions, and postconditions.



Description: Algorithms on arrays require expressing global properties:

Sorted: increasing or decreasing order of elements.
Permutation: preservation of the multiset of elements (same occurrences, possibly different order).
Sub-array: properties over index segments.




Description: Hoare logic allows decomposing the proof of program correctness by verifying triples {P} C {Q}. For loops, an invariant is used. Why3 automates the generation of proof obligations (verification conditions) from annotated code.





De Morgan’s Laws: \(\neg (A \land B) \equiv \neg A \lor \neg B\) \(\neg (A \lor B) \equiv \neg A \land \neg B\)
Implication Elimination: \(A \Rightarrow B \equiv \neg A \lor B\)
Distributivity: \(A \land (B \lor C) \equiv (A \land B) \lor (A \land C)\) \(A \lor (B \land C) \equiv (A \lor B) \land (A \lor C)\)
Quantifiers: \(\forall i, P(i)\): for all \(i\), \(P(i)\) is true. \(\exists i, P(i)\): there exists \(i\) such that \(P(i)\) is true. \(\neg \forall i, P(i) \equiv \exists i, \neg P(i)\) \(\neg \exists i, P(i) \equiv \forall i, \neg P(i)\)
Hoare Triple: \(\{P\} \; C \; \{Q\}\) means: if execution of \(C\) begins in a state satisfying \(P\), and if \(C\) terminates, then the final state satisfies \(Q\).






Context: Binary search in a sorted array.
Application:
The pseudocode for binary search is given. The precondition requires that the input array be sorted:
\[
\forall i,j \in \{0,\ldots,n-1\},\; i \leq j \Rightarrow a[i] \leq a[j]
\]
The postcondition specifies the result res:
\[
\big(res \in \{0,\ldots,n-1\} \wedge a[res] = elem\big) \;\vee\; \big(res = -1 \wedge \forall i \in \{0,\ldots,n-1\}, a[i] \neq elem\big)
\]
This guarantees that if the element is present, res is a valid index where it is found; otherwise res is \(-1\) and the element is absent.



Context: Binary search, while loop.
Application:
The proposed invariant is:
\[
I_1 \;=\; 0 \leq l \;\wedge\; u \leq n-1 \;\wedge\; \forall i \in \{0,\ldots,n-1\},\; a[i] = elem \Rightarrow l \leq i \leq u
\]
where l and u are the current bounds of the search interval.
Interpretation:

The bounds l and u remain within the array limits (or at the edges).
If the element elem is present in the array, then it must be within the interval [l, u].

At each iteration, the middle m is computed. Depending on the comparison between a[m] and elem, l or u is updated to preserve the invariant. When the loop terminates (l > u), the postcondition can be concluded.



Context: Bubble sort.
Application:
